questions.question: A matrix with equal number of rows and columns is called a:
questions.explanation: A square matrix has the same number of rows and columns (n × n). Examples: 2×2, 3×3 matrices.

questions.question: If A is a 2×3 matrix and B is a 3×2 matrix, then AB is a matrix of order:
questions.explanation: For matrix multiplication AB, if A is m×n and B is n×p, then AB is m×p. Here A is 2×3, B is 3×2, so AB is 2×2.

questions.question: The transpose of a matrix A is obtained by:
questions.explanation: The transpose A^T of a matrix A is obtained by interchanging its rows and columns. If A is m×n, then A^T is n×m.

questions.question: A symmetric matrix satisfies:
questions.explanation: A matrix A is symmetric if A = A^T (it equals its own transpose). In a symmetric matrix, aᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ for all i, j.

questions.question: Matrix multiplication is generally:
questions.explanation: Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general: AB ≠ BA. It is, however, associative: A(BC) = (AB)C.

questions.question: If det(A) = 0, the matrix A is called:
questions.explanation: A matrix with determinant = 0 is called singular. A singular matrix has no inverse.

questions.question: The identity matrix I has the property that for any square matrix A:
questions.explanation: The identity matrix I satisfies AI = IA = A. It acts as the multiplicative identity for matrices, analogous to 1 in ordinary multiplication.

questions.question: The area of a triangle with vertices (x₁,y₁), (x₂,y₂), (x₃,y₃) using determinants is:
questions.explanation: Area = ½|det| where the determinant uses the coordinates. This equals ½|x₁(y₂−y₃) + x₂(y₃−y₁) + x₃(y₁−y₂)|.

questions.question: If any two rows (or columns) of a determinant are identical, its value is:
questions.explanation: A property of determinants: if any two rows (or columns) are identical, the value of the determinant is 0.

questions.question: The cofactor Cᵢⱼ of element aᵢⱼ in a matrix is:
options: The determinant of the entire matrix
questions.explanation: Cofactor Cᵢⱼ = (−1)^(i+j) × Mᵢⱼ, where Mᵢⱼ is the minor (determinant of the submatrix after removing row i and column j).

questions.question: The system of equations AX = B has a unique solution when:
questions.explanation: By Cramer's rule and the inverse method: AX = B has a unique solution X = A⁻¹B when det(A) ≠ 0 (A is non-singular).

questions.question: If A is a 3×3 matrix and det(A) = 5, then det(3A) =
questions.explanation: det(kA) = k^n × det(A) where n is the order of the matrix. det(3A) = 3³ × 5 = 27 × 5 = 135.

questions.question: Interchanging two rows of a determinant:
questions.explanation: Exchanging any two rows (or columns) of a determinant changes the sign of the determinant (multiplies it by −1).

questions.question: The inverse of a non-singular matrix A is given by:
questions.explanation: A⁻¹ = adj(A)/det(A), where adj(A) is the adjugate (transpose of cofactor matrix). This only exists when det(A) ≠ 0.
